bars.bar: L1 Accuracy: chemistry model error at least 3% below the sum-of-parts line
L2 Consistency: beats the sum-of-parts line in 6+ of 9 seasons
L3 Parts matter: sum-of-parts error at least 5% below the league average guess
L4 Chemistry finder: top 10% vs bottom 10% expected-gain lineups differ by 1.0+ per 100
L6 Not luck: real gain beats 95% of 200 shuffles
bars.result: beat 100% of shuffles, but the real gain is -0.1%, below zero

bars.bar: L7 Familiarity: lineups with 4-5 returning players beat parts by 0.5+ more than 0-2 returning, in 6+ of 9 seasons

verdict: Last year's player ratings predict how a lineup will play, and the line from the sum of the five ratings is the one to trust. The chemistry model, which adds position mix, star power, balance and continuity, did no better than that line (it was slightly worse), so these structure features do not predict which lineups beat their parts. The one thing that showed up is familiarity: lineups built from players who were together the year before beat their parts in 7 of 9 seasons, by about 2 points per 100 possessions on average. Because coaches keep playing lineups that work, the lineups in the gap tables below are the ones that survived, so big gaps are partly selection and partly luck.
learned: What the model weighed: the sum of the five ratings carries almost everything. Offense and star power add a little, and the number of returning players is the one structure feature with a clear positive sign. Position counts and age add nothing reliable.
